newsitem.title: INDONESIA: IMF tells ASEAN to cut deficits, increase savings.
newsitem.headline: IMF tells ASEAN to cut deficits, increase savings.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund said on Thursday the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) should reduce current account deficits and increase savings rates to combat external vulnerability.

Michel Camdessus, managing director of the Washington-based IMF, said at the start of a two-day conference on macro-economic issues, that it was paradoxical to call for increased savings in the seven ASEAN member countries, which have the highest savings rates in the world.
But he stressed there was scope to do even better.

"It would help address the challenge posed by capital inflows, reduce the burden on monetary policy and tend to reduce interest rates. All of which would help safeguard macroeconomic stability," Camdessus said.
ASEAN comprises Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines, Vietnam and Brunei.
Large net private capital inflows had tended to raise aggregate expenditures, increase inflationary pressures and widen current account deficits in all recipient countries.
Camdessus said policies must be geared to achieve those targets over the longer-term to reduce reliance on foreign savings and strengthen public savings.
However, he said this did not mean that combating inflation was no longer high on the IMF agenda, although fighting inflation was not the centrepiece of his speech.
"This (fighting inflation) is my obsession. This is my justification in life," Camdessus said.
"Inflation is a seven-headed dragon. When you have cut off six of his heads, you have not done anything yet," he said.
"Low inflation creates the basis for a sustainable rate of growth and also a sustainable rate of domestic savings, so is the key for long-term development," Camdessus said.
He said he believed there was still room for most nations in the region to adopt an even more ambitious approach to fiscal consolidation.
"There is always scope to reduce costly investment incentives and unproductive outlays," he said.
Camdessus noted military expenditure in the region had risen, while worldwide military spending relative to GDP declined between 1991 and 1994.
Military spending in Asian developing countries, including Southeast Asia, had remained the same or increased despite rapid GDP growth in most of these countries, he said.
Camdessus said the greatest threat to stability was posed by more volatile short-term capital inflows.
ASEAN countries had been the centre for foreign investments looking for high returns and healthy fundamentals. But they had, at the same time, increasingly complicated monetary management.
ASEAN's share of total foreign investment received by developing countries was estimated at an average of about 25 percent during the 1990s, compared with just a trickle in the 1970s.
Camdessus said direct quantitative controls on capital inflows had rarely worked for any sustained period and could run counter to the thrust of external liberalisation.
He said fiscal consolidation can also play a role in discouraging speculative inflows by providing greater scope for short-term flexibility in exchange rate policy.
"Indonesia, for example, has moved in this direction," he noted.
Indonesia's central bank had widened its band in September to eight percent from five percent for the dollar-rupiah rate, one of the widest in the region.
